problem: Prior navigation systems usually handle one goal modality (object category, image, or language) and one goal per episode, and are evaluated mostly in simulation. None of them keeps an instance-level memory that separates different objects of the same category, so none can reach a sequence of category, image and language goals in real homes while reusing what it has already seen.
motivation: Robots in homes and warehouses run for long periods and receive goals phrased the way people naturally phrase them: 'a SINK', a photo, or 'the potted plant next to the couch'. They should get faster as they learn the environment. The design draws on cognitive maps and landmark-based navigation in animals and humans: keep a metric map plus raw visual views of object instances, so the memory can be queried with either images or text.
key_idea: A modular system with a continually growing, instance-aware Object Instance Memory: a top-down semantic map plus the raw image views of each detected object instance. Image goals are matched against it with SuperGlue keypoints and language goals with CLIP, restricted to instances of the goal's category. Matched instances become point-navigation targets; if nothing matches, the robot does frontier exploration.
insight:
Two things drive the gains: keeping instance-level identity and keeping memory across goals.
- **Instance identity:** GOAT w/o Instances (nearest object of the right category) keeps category SR at 94.1 but collapses on image and language goals (28.6 / 27.6 SR vs 86.4 / 68.2).
- **Memory across goals:** GOAT w/o Memory drops SPL from 0.642 to 0.188. Full GOAT rises from 60% SR at the first goal to 90% for goals 5-10.
- **Matching design (offline Table 2):** storing raw views lets each modality use its best matcher. Restricting candidates to the goal's category adds ~23%, padded bounding boxes add ~22% over tight boxes, SuperGlue beats CLIP for image goals by ~13%, and max-over-views is the best aggregation. A fixed threshold during exploration costs ~6%, so matching gets better after full exploration.
- **Detector:** a 2017 COCO Mask R-CNN was more reliable than open-vocabulary detectors (Detic, OWL-ViT, LSeg) for common categories in the real world.
method: Perception: a COCO-pretrained Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50) segments instances. Depth holes (e.g. reflective objects) are filled with MiDaS monocular depth, rescaled via a least-squares affine fit (A, b) to the valid sensor depth. The segmentation is projected to a point cloud, binned into a 3D semantic voxel map, and summed over height into a 2D instance map.

Semantic map: a K×M×M grid with 5 cm cells. K = C category channels (storing instance IDs) + 4 channels (obstacles, explored area, current and past agent location). It is initialized at episode start and kept across goals (lifelong).

Object Instance Memory: each detection is dilated by p cells. It merges with an existing instance if the category matches and the dilated cells overlap; otherwise it becomes a new instance. Each instance stores its map cells, its category, and a set of context-padded bounding-box image crops (views).

Global policy / goal matching: category goals check the semantic map for any object of that category. Language goals get their category from Mistral 7B, then CLIP cosine similarity against views of that category's instances. Image goals get their category from Mask R-CNN, then SuperGlue keypoint matching. Scores take the max over views; a threshold applies during exploration and the argmax is used once the environment is fully explored.

Exploration and local policy: with no match, frontier-based exploration picks the closest unexplored region. The Fast Marching Method plans to the long-term goal. Spot follows waypoints with its built-in point-nav controller; Stretch executes the first discrete action (forward / turn) along the path.
People as instances: persons are handled as PERSON-category image instances. Their stale locations are cleared from the map, which gives social navigation (avoid or follow people).

setting.backbone: Modular, all frozen: Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50, COCO-pretrained) for detection, CLIP for language-image matching, SuperGlue for image-image matching, MiDaS for depth infill, Mistral 7B for extracting a category from a language goal. Mapping, exploration and planning are classical (frontier exploration + Fast Marching Method).
setting.model_size: Largest component is Mistral 7B (category extraction only); the others are small pretrained vision models
setting.training_data: none (training-free; off-the-shelf pretrained models, no navigation training)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + pose from onboard SLAM; goal given as category label, image, or language description
setting.action_space: long-term point goals on a top-down map, planned with FMM. Spot: waypoints to its built-in point-nav controller. Stretch: discrete move forward / turn left / turn right.
setting.privileged: none (no pre-computed maps or object locations)

numbers_note:
All results come from the paper's own real-world protocol, not from a standard simulator benchmark. Note: 'GOAT' here is not the later simulated GOAT-Bench. Split is labelled 'test' by convention (unseen homes).
- SPL values are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.642) and converted to 0-100.
- The per-sequential-goal curves (Fig. 3) are figure-only apart from the quoted 60%/90% SR and 0.20/0.80 SPL.
- Text says GOAT w/o Memory 'achieves 61% success rate', but Table 1 prints 60.3.
- Matching thresholds are inconsistent across sections. Methods: 0.28 CLIP / 6.0 SuperGlue. Supplementary text: 3.0 SuperGLUE / 0.75 language CLIP. Table 2: 0.75 image CLIP / 0.26 language CLIP.
- The CLIP-on-Wheels baseline got SR 50.7 / SPL 0.418 (baseline, not listed above).
results: Over 90 real-world episodes in 9 homes, GOAT reached 83.0% average SR and 0.642 SPL (86.4 / 68.2 / 94.3% SR for image / language / category goals). The strongest baseline, CLIP on Wheels, got 50.7% SR and 0.418 SPL. GOAT w/o Instances got 49.4% SR and GOAT w/o Memory got 60.3% SR / 0.188 SPL. SR improves with experience, from 60% at the first goal to 90% for goals 5-10. The same policy transfers to pick-and-place (79% object / 87% receptacle finding) and social navigation (81% SR with moving people, 83% person following).
limitations: Language-goal matching with CLIP is much weaker than SuperGlue image matching (68.2 vs 86.4 SR; ~23% gap offline), because CLIP misses fine-grained instance attributes. It also relies on a closed-vocabulary COCO Mask R-CNN limited to 15 goal categories, since open-vocabulary detectors were less reliable.
Matching during exploration depends on hand-tuned score thresholds, which cause false positives and false negatives. Performance is clearly better only after the environment is fully explored.

The evaluation is a custom real-world protocol (quantitative results only on Spot, using its built-in controller and SLAM pose), so it is hard to reproduce or compare with simulation benchmarks. The world is assumed mostly static except for people.
